questions.question: When selecting baselines for finetuning a large generative model, which criterion best ensures a fair comparison?
questions.choice_A: Match the total trainable parameter count or compute budget across methods and tune hyperparameters to comparable validation performance targets.
questions.choice_B: Use the most popular baseline from recent papers without adjusting any hyperparameters.
questions.choice_C: Compare to the largest available model, regardless of resource constraints.
questions.choice_D: Choose baselines that produce similar qualitative outputs on a few cherry-picked examples.

questions.question: Which practice most effectively reduces data leakage when defining dataset splits?
questions.choice_A: Randomly sampling training, validation, and test sets at the start of each epoch.
questions.choice_B: Creating stable, disjoint splits once and ensuring that near-duplicate or paraphrased items do not cross splits.
questions.choice_C: Using the same examples for validation and test to reduce variance in evaluation.
questions.choice_D: Expanding the test set with training examples to improve statistical power.

questions.question: In few-shot prompting experiments, which consideration is most important for comparability across methods?
questions.choice_A: Using the longest possible context to maximize information.
questions.choice_B: Varying the number of shots between models to match their parameter counts.
questions.choice_C: Standardizing the prompt template and number/order of shots across all models and reporting sensitivity to shot selection.
questions.choice_D: Selecting demonstration examples that each model performs best on.

questions.question: You are comparing LoRA ranks across finetuning runs. What is the main reason to perform an ablation over rank values (e.g., $r \in \{4, 8, 16, 32\}$)?
questions.choice_A: To ensure that training always converges faster for higher ranks.
questions.choice_B: To verify that the base model architecture is optimal.
questions.choice_C: To prove that rank does not affect generalization at all.
questions.choice_D: To quantify the accuracy–capacity–compute trade-off as rank increases and identify diminishing returns.

questions.question: What is the best practice for reporting results over multiple random seeds?
questions.choice_A: Report mean and standard deviation across sufficient seeds and justify the chosen number of seeds.
questions.choice_B: Report only the best seed to highlight potential performance.
questions.choice_C: Use a single seed but repeat training three times with the same seed.
questions.choice_D: Average results across seeds without reporting dispersion.

questions.question: Which failure mode should be explicitly discussed in generative model papers to aid reproducibility and understanding?
questions.choice_A: Only those failures that occur in the final model checkpoint.
questions.choice_B: Typical failure cases such as mode collapse, prompt sensitivity, and instability during training with representative examples.
questions.choice_C: Failures that affect competitors’ methods but not your own.
questions.choice_D: No failures, because they might confuse readers.

questions.question: When matching parameter budgets across methods, which comparison is most appropriate?
questions.choice_A: Comparing a full-model finetune with 100% of parameters updated to a LoRA finetune with 1% trainable parameters.
questions.choice_B: Comparing models by wall-clock time on different GPUs.
questions.choice_C: Budgeting by either total trainable parameters or total training FLOPs and aligning optimizer states and sequence lengths.
questions.choice_D: Comparing any two methods as long as they use the same learning rate.

questions.question: Which practice best supports reproducibility for computational environments?
questions.choice_A: Listing the operating system but not library versions.
questions.choice_B: Describing the GPU type but omitting CUDA/cuDNN details.
questions.choice_C: Providing a Dockerfile or Conda environment with pinned package versions and documenting hardware, CUDA, and driver versions.
questions.choice_D: Stating that any modern environment should work.

questions.question: In data-efficiency experiments, what should be reported to make conclusions robust?
questions.choice_A: The learning curves over multiple dataset fractions with confidence intervals or error bars.
questions.choice_C: A single point at full data only.
questions.choice_D: Only the largest dataset size due to stability.

questions.question: Which approach to hyperparameter tuning is fairest across baselines?
questions.choice_A: Spend more tuning budget on your proposed method to show its full potential.
questions.choice_B: Allocate a comparable tuning budget (e.g., number of trials or compute) for each baseline and use the same validation protocol.
questions.choice_C: Adopt hyperparameters from unrelated tasks for all methods.
questions.choice_D: Tune only the learning rate for baselines but all hyperparameters for your method.

questions.question: Why should you report both parameter counts and activation memory considerations when discussing model size?
questions.choice_A: Activation memory determines inference speed but not training feasibility.
questions.choice_B: Parameter count always predicts VRAM usage during training exactly.
questions.choice_C: Training memory depends on activations, sequence length, and optimizer states, not just parameter count; this affects fairness and feasibility.
questions.choice_D: Activation memory is negligible for long-context models.

questions.question: Which statement about random seeds is most accurate for generative model experiments?
questions.choice_A: Using a fixed seed ensures identical results across different hardware.
questions.choice_B: Seeds must be hidden to prevent overfitting.
questions.choice_C: Reporting seeds, seeding all relevant libraries, and noting any non-deterministic ops helps others reproduce results.
questions.choice_D: Seeding the dataloader alone is sufficient.

questions.question: What is a sound strategy to avoid prompt leakage between train and test in instruction tuning?
questions.choice_A: Use the same template but different tasks for train and test without checking overlap.
questions.choice_B: Ensure that task templates, instructions, and near-duplicate prompts are excluded from the test split and document the filtering.
questions.choice_C: Randomize token order in prompts during testing.
questions.choice_D: Increase temperature during testing to mask leakage.

questions.question: When conducting ablations over transformer block choices (e.g., which layers to finetune), what should be reported?
questions.choice_A: Only the best-performing layer subset.
questions.choice_B: Performance across different layer subsets (e.g., top-k, bottom-k, interleaved), along with trainable parameter counts and compute.
questions.choice_C: Ablations only on the middle layers, as they are most representative.
questions.choice_D: Which layers are easiest to code with.

questions.question: How should decoding settings be handled to ensure fair comparison across generative models?
questions.choice_A: Use different sampling temperatures per model to maximize each model’s performance on the test set.
questions.choice_B: Tune decoding on the test set for each model.
questions.choice_C: Fix or validate decoding parameters (e.g., temperature, top-$p$, max tokens) on a validation set and apply consistently to the test set.
questions.choice_D: Leave decoding at default library settings for all models, regardless of mismatch.

questions.question: What is the rationale for reporting standard deviations rather than only means in benchmark tables?
questions.choice_A: It reduces the number of runs needed.
questions.choice_B: It allows selecting the best run without justification.
questions.choice_C: It quantifies variability across seeds or folds and helps assess whether differences are practically meaningful.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees statistically significant differences.

questions.question: Which practice improves transparency about compute when presenting results?
questions.choice_A: Reporting only GPU model names.
questions.choice_B: Reporting total training time, number/type of accelerators, precision (e.g., FP16/bfloat16), sequence lengths, and gradient accumulation settings.
questions.choice_C: Reporting that training was done 'in the cloud' without further details.
questions.choice_D: Providing only energy consumption estimates.

questions.question: In few-shot evaluations, which control best isolates the effect of the number of shots?
questions.choice_A: Changing both the number of shots and the prompt template simultaneously.
questions.choice_B: Keeping the template, order, and content of shots fixed while varying only the number of demonstrations and averaging over multiple shot subsets.
questions.choice_C: Selecting shots that each model answers correctly.
questions.choice_D: Sampling new shots from the test set.

questions.question: How should you handle public code release for reproducibility?
questions.choice_A: Release only the final weights; code is unnecessary.
questions.choice_B: Release code with an environment file, scripts to reproduce results end-to-end (including data preprocessing), and document exact checkpoints/tokenizers.
questions.choice_C: Release code without instructions to prevent misuse.
questions.choice_D: Release a high-level description instead of code to save space.

questions.question: Which evaluation protocol best mitigates the effect of pretraining contamination on reported performance?
questions.choice_A: Assume no contamination if the base model is widely used.
questions.choice_B: Only evaluate on leaderboards.
questions.choice_C: Use contamination-checked test sets, report any overlap analysis performed, and supplement with held-out, freshly curated data when possible.
questions.choice_D: Increase model temperature during evaluation.

questions.question: When reporting negative results from ablation studies, what is most informative?
questions.choice_A: Omit them to keep the paper concise.
questions.choice_B: Report that changes 'did not work' without details.
questions.choice_C: Provide the experimental setup, values tried, metrics with variances, and hypotheses for why the changes underperformed.
questions.choice_D: Mention them only in informal blog posts.
